b2015-1.ask: Which figure has exactly half of its area shaded?
steps: Check each figure: what fraction is shaded?
The circle has 1 of 3 equal parts shaded: 1/3. The square C has 3 of 4 parts: 3/4.
The square D has 1 of 4 triangles: 1/4. The pentagon has 2 of 5 parts: 2/5.
The triangle B is split down the middle into two equal halves, one shaded: 1/2.
b2015-1.check: Fold triangle B along its middle line: the shaded half covers the white half exactly. ✓
b2015-1.spot: Fractions of shapes? Count the equal parts, then the shaded ones.
b2015-1.oops: Counting parts that aren't the same size.

b2015-2.ask: An umbrella has KANGAROO written around it. Which picture does NOT show this umbrella?
steps: Read the letters around the umbrella in order: K-A-N-G-A-R-O-O, then back to K.
Any view shows a few letters next to each other, in that order, going round the same way.
Check each picture (turn it upside down if that helps): ANG, OOK, NGA and ARO are all real pieces of the ring.
Picture C reads backwards: its letters go round the wrong way. So it can't be this umbrella.
b2015-2.check: Turn picture C halfway round: it still doesn't match any stretch of KANGAROO. ✓
b2015-2.spot: Which view is impossible? Look for a mirrored letter or a wrong order.
b2015-2.oops: Only checking which letters appear, not which way round they go.

b2015-3.ask: 9 squares are painted black, white and gray. Fewest squares to repaint so no two touching squares match?
steps: Find the touching pairs with the same colour.
In the top row, two gray squares touch. In the bottom row, two black squares touch.
These two problems are in different rows and don't share a square, so one repaint can't fix both.
Repaint the top-right square black and the bottom-middle square gray: 2 repaints, and now no two touching squares match.
b2015-3.check: After 2 repaints, check every touching pair: all different. ✓
b2015-3.spot: Fewest changes? Find all the problems first, then see if one change can fix more than one.
b2015-3.oops: Repainting a square without checking it doesn't create a new match.

b2015-4.ask: 5 ducks lay an egg every day, 5 lay every other day. How many eggs in 10 days?
steps: Everyday ducks: 5 ducks × 10 days = 50 eggs.
Every-other-day ducks lay on 5 of the 10 days: 5 ducks × 5 = 25 eggs.
b2015-4.check: Each day: 5 eggs, plus 5 more every second day. 10 × 5 + 5 × 5 = 75. ✓
b2015-4.spot: Groups doing things at different rates? Work out each group, then add.

b2015-5.ask: Each small square has area 4 cm². How long is the thick black line?
steps: Area 4 cm² means each side is 2 cm (2 × 2 = 4).
The thick line runs along the sides of the small squares. Count how many sides it uses: 9.
9 sides × 2 cm = 18 cm.
b2015-5.check: Count again, carefully following the line from one end to the other. ✓
b2015-5.spot: Area of a square given? First find the side length.
b2015-5.oops: Using 4 cm as the side. 4 is the area.

steps: A fraction is smaller than 2 if the top is less than 2 times the bottom.
19/8: 2 × 8 = 16, and 19 > 16. Bigger than 2. Same for 20/9, 21/10 and 22/11 (that one is exactly 2).
b2015-6.spot: Comparing fractions with a whole number? Multiply the bottom by that number.
b2015-6.oops: Thinking the biggest numbers make the biggest fraction.

b2015-7.ask: Pumpkin + watermelon = 8 kg. The watermelon is 2 kg lighter. How heavy is the pumpkin?
steps: Pretend the watermelon were 2 kg heavier: then both would weigh the same as the pumpkin.
The total would be 8 + 2 = 10 kg for 2 pumpkins.
One pumpkin = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 kg.
b2015-7.spot: Two things with a total and a difference? Even them out first, then split.
b2015-7.oops: Splitting 8 into 4 and 4 and ignoring the difference.

b2015-8.ask: Each plant has either 5 leaves, or 2 leaves and 1 flower. Altogether: 6 flowers and 32 leaves. How many plants?
steps: 6 flowers means 6 flowering plants. They have 6 × 2 = 12 leaves.
The other leaves: 32 − 12 = 20, all on 5-leaf plants.
20 ÷ 5 = 4 plants with 5 leaves.
Total: 6 + 4 = 10 plants.
b2015-8.spot: Two kinds of things? Use the clue that only fits one kind (flowers) first.
b2015-8.oops: Forgetting the flowering plants also have leaves.

b2015-9.ask: Two equal strips overlapping 10 cm make 50 cm. With two more of the same strips, how much overlap gives 56 cm?
steps: Two strips with 10 cm overlap = 50 cm. With no overlap they'd be 50 + 10 = 60 cm.
So two strips laid end to end are 60 cm (each is 30 cm).
To get 56 cm, the overlap must eat up 60 − 56 = 4 cm.
b2015-9.spot: Overlaps? Total length = both pieces − the overlap.
b2015-9.oops: Thinking a longer strip needs a longer overlap. It's the other way round.

b2015-10.ask: 6 unit squares make a stepped shape (1 on top, 2 in the middle, 3 on the bottom). What's its perimeter?
steps: Count the up-and-down edges and the across edges separately.
Up-and-down: every row has one edge on its left end and one on its right end. 3 rows × 2 = 6.
Across: the bottom is 3 long. The top of the bottom row sticks out by 1 in total (half on each side). The top of the middle row sticks out by 1. The very top is 1. That's 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6.
b2015-10.check: Count the edges again starting from a different corner: still 12. ✓
b2015-10.spot: Perimeter of square shapes? Walk all the way around, counting each edge once.
b2015-10.oops: Counting inside lines as part of the perimeter.

b2015-12.ask: Rectangle ABCD is made of 4 equal small rectangles. BC = 1 cm. How long is AB?
steps: Look at the picture: a standing rectangle on the left, two lying rectangles stacked in the middle, and a standing one on the right.
The standing rectangles' long side = the height BC = 1 cm.
The two lying rectangles stacked make the same height: 2 short sides = 1 cm, so a short side is 0.5 cm.
AB = short (left) + long (middle) + short (right) = 0.5 + 1 + 0.5 = 2 cm.
b2015-12.check: Each small rectangle is 1 by 0.5, and they fit together exactly. ✓
b2015-12.spot: Equal pieces in a picture? Label the short and long sides and match them up.
b2015-12.oops: Thinking all the rectangles are the same way round.

b2015-14.ask: Lucy and her mom were both born in February. On March 19, 2015, she adds both birth years and both ages. What's the total?
steps: After your birthday each year, birth year + age = this year. Example: born 2005, age 10 in 2015: 2005 + 10 = 2015.
Both birthdays (in February) have already happened by March 19.
So Lucy's year + age = 2015, and Mom's year + age = 2015.
b2015-14.check: Try any example: Lucy born 2006 (age 9), Mom born 1980 (age 35): 2006 + 1980 + 9 + 35 = 4030. ✓
b2015-14.spot: Birth year and age together? They add up to this year (if the birthday has passed).
b2015-14.oops: Trying to guess their actual ages. You don't need them.

b2015-15.ask: A number divided by 9 leaves 7. What's left over when twice that number is divided by 9?
steps: The number is some 9s plus 7 left over.
Doubling it doubles the 9s (still fits into 9s) and doubles the leftover: 7 + 7 = 14.
14 is one more 9 with 5 left over.
b2015-15.spot: Remainders? Only the leftover matters. Do the math on the leftover.
b2015-15.oops: Answering 14. A remainder must be smaller than 9.

b2015-17.ask: Colour each segment red, green or blue so every triangle has three different colours. Some are already coloured. What colour is x?
steps: Call the four triangles A, B, C and D. Start where two sides are already known.
The side shared by A and B can't be blue or red (those are used next to it), so it's green.
Triangle B now has green and red, so its last side is blue. The side shared by C and D can't be blue or red, so it's green.
Triangle C now has green and blue, so its last side, x, must be red.
b2015-17.check: Fill in the whole picture: every triangle has red, green and blue. ✓
b2015-17.spot: Colouring with rules? Start where the most is known, and let each answer unlock the next.

b2015-18.ask: 3 green apples, 5 yellow apples, 7 green pears, 2 yellow pears. Fewest fruits to be sure of an apple and a pear of the same colour?
steps: Be unlucky Ulysses: what's the most you can take WITHOUT a matching apple and pear?
Take all 5 yellow apples and all 7 green pears. Yellow apples need a yellow pear, green pears need a green apple. No match!
That's 12 fruits with no match.
The 13th fruit is a green apple or a yellow pear, which makes a match.
b2015-18.spot: 'To be sure'? Find the unluckiest grab, then add one.
b2015-18.oops: Taking all the apples first (8). Mixing colours is unluckier.

b2015-19.ask: A 'kangaroo' chess piece jumps 3 one way and 1 the other way. Fewest moves to reach square A?
steps: Find where the kangaroo can get in 1 move (the arrows). A isn't one of them.
From each of those squares, find where it can get in another move. A still isn't reachable in 2.
Try 3 moves: there's a path that lands on A.
So the fewest is 3.
b2015-19.check: Trace the 3 jumps on the board: each is 3 + 1 squares. ✓
b2015-19.spot: Fewest moves? Check 1 move, then 2, then 3, until you reach it.
b2015-19.oops: Thinking it's close, so 2 moves must work. Close squares can be the hardest to reach.

b2015-20.ask: X + X + YY = ZZZ, where each letter is a different digit. What is X?
steps: The biggest X + X + YY can be is 9 + 9 + 99 = 117.
ZZZ has three equal digits and is at most 117, so it's 111. Z = 1.
YY must be 99 or 88 (to get near 111). 111 − 99 = 12, so X + X = 12, X = 6.
(111 − 88 = 23 can't be split into two equal digits.)
b2015-20.spot: Letter puzzles? Find the biggest or smallest possible total first.
b2015-20.oops: Forgetting each letter must be a different digit.

b2015-21.ask: Four whole numbers add to 39. Two of them multiply to 80, and the other two also multiply to 80. What's the biggest number?
steps: List every pair that multiplies to 80: 1 × 80, 2 × 40, 4 × 20, 5 × 16, 8 × 10.
Two pairs must add to 39. 21 + 18 = 39! So the numbers are 5, 16, 8 and 10.
The biggest is 16.
b2015-21.spot: Numbers with a known product? List all the factor pairs.

b2015-22.ask: Jane spent half her money + $1 on book 1, half the rest + $2 on book 2, half the rest + $3 on book 3, and then had nothing. How much did the books cost?
steps: Rewind from the end. After book 3: $0. Book 3 cost half + $3, so the other half was $3. Before book 3 she had $6.
Book 2: she had some money, spent half + $2, and $6 was left. So half − $2 = $6, half = $8. Before book 2: $16.
Book 1: spent half + $1, $16 left. Half = $17. Before book 1: $34.
She spent everything, so the books cost $34.
b2015-22.check: Forwards: 34 → spend 17 + 1 = 18, left 16 → spend 8 + 2 = 10, left 6 → spend 3 + 3 = 6, left 0. 18 + 10 + 6 = 34. ✓
b2015-22.spot: Spending in steps until nothing's left? Rewind from the end.
b2015-22.oops: Undoing 'half + 1' as 'half − 1'. Write it out carefully.

b2015-23.ask: 9 houses, at least 1 person each, two neighbouring houses have at most 6 together. Most people possible?
steps: Big houses next to small ones: a house of 5 next to a house of 1 makes 6.
Pattern: 5, 1, 5, 1, 5, 1, 5, 1, 5. Start and end with 5 to fit five 5s.
b2015-23.check: Pair houses 1–2, 3–4, 5–6, 7–8: at most 6 each = 24. House 9 at most 5. 24 + 5 = 29. ✓
b2015-23.spot: Limit on neighbours? Alternate big and small, and start and end with big.

b2015-25.ask: In the 4-digit number abcd, a < b < c < d. What's the biggest bd − ac?
steps: bd − ac = 10 × (b − a) + (d − c). The tens part matters most, so make b − a as big as possible.
a must be at least 1 (it starts a number). c and d must be bigger than b, so b can be at most 7 (with c = 8, d = 9).
b2015-25.check: Try b = 6 instead: 69 − 17 = 52. Smaller. With b = 7 you get the biggest tens part, so 61 is the best. ✓
b2015-25.spot: Biggest difference of 2-digit numbers? Focus on the tens digits first.
b2015-25.oops: Forgetting that c and d must be bigger than b.

b2015-26.ask: Each vertex of a cube gets the sum of its three faces. C = 14, D = 16, E = 24. What's F?
steps: C and D are next to each other. They share two faces; C has the right face and D has the left face.
So C − D = right face − left face = 14 − 16 = −2.
E and F are also next to each other, the same way: F has the right face, E has the left face.
So F − E = right − left = −2. F = 24 − 2 = 22.
b2015-26.check: The difference between neighbours along that direction is always the same: right minus left. ✓
b2015-26.spot: Sums that share parts? Take away what they share.
b2015-26.oops: Trying to find every face's number. You don't need to.

b2015-27.ask: Every train car has the same number of compartments. Compartment 50 is in the 7th car. How many compartments per car?
steps: The first 6 cars hold fewer than 50 compartments (or 50 would be in car 6 or earlier).
7 cars hold at least 50.
Try 7 per car: 7 cars = 49. Not enough. Try 8: 6 cars = 48 (less than 50) and 7 cars = 56 (at least 50). ✓
Try 9: 6 cars = 54, so 50 would be in car 6. ✗. So 8.
b2015-27.check: Car 7 holds compartments 49 to 56, and 50 is one of them. ✓
b2015-27.spot: Which group is item N in? Test choices: the groups before must hold fewer than N.

b2015-28.ask: In a strip of 7 cells, colour 3 cells so no two coloured cells touch. How many ways?
steps: Make a neat list, left to right. Name the cells 1 to 7.
Starting with 1, 3: then 5, 6 or 7 (3 ways). 1, 4: then 6 or 7 (2 ways). 1, 5: then 7 (1 way).
Starting with 2, 4: then 6 or 7 (2 ways). 2, 5: 7 (1 way).
Starting with 3, 5, 7: 1 way. Total: 3 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 10.
b2015-28.check: Every set in the list has gaps between the cells, and none is listed twice. ✓
b2015-28.spot: Counting arrangements? Use an ordered list so nothing is missed or doubled.
b2015-28.oops: Listing randomly and missing a few.

b2015-29.ask: Four points on a line. The 6 distances between them, in order, are 2, 3, k, 11, 12, 14. What is k?
steps: The biggest distance, 14, is from the first point to the last. The three gaps between neighbouring points add to 14.
The smallest distances, 2 and 3, must be gaps between neighbours.
14 − 2 = 12 and 14 − 3 = 11: these are on the list, so 2 and 3 are the two END gaps.
The middle gap is 14 − 2 − 3 = 9. Distances: 2, 3, 9, 11, 12, 14. So k = 9.
b2015-29.spot: Distances between points on a line? Draw it and label the gaps.
b2015-29.oops: Putting 2 and 3 next to each other in the middle.

b2015-30.ask: A 4 × 4 × 4 cube has 3 faces painted red and 3 blue. No small cube has 3 red faces. How many small cubes have both red and blue?
steps: If three red faces met at a corner, that corner cube would have 3 red faces. So the red faces are two opposite faces plus one more (like top, bottom and front). Blue is left, right and back.
Every corner cube touches 3 faces, and none can be all red or all blue. All 8 corners have both colours.
Edges between a red face and a blue face: 8 of the 12 edges. Each edge has 2 middle cubes: 8 × 2 = 16.
b2015-30.check: Edges between two red faces (2) or two blue faces (2) don't count. 2 + 2 + 8 = 12 edges ✓.
b2015-30.spot: Painted cubes? Corners touch 3 faces, edges 2, middles 1.
b2015-30.oops: Forgetting to count the corner cubes.
